response.title: Which lithium battery can sit in an unheated off-grid cabin through a freezing winter with solar still charging it and nobody there?
response.answer:
For an unheated off-grid cabin that sits unattended all winter while solar panels keep charging, my recommendation is a self-heating LiFePO₄ (lithium iron phosphate) battery with automatic low-temperature charge protection.

But there's an important distinction: a lithium battery that can survive freezing temperatures is not necessarily one that can charge safely while frozen.

What you need

A suitable battery should have:

Automatic low-temperature charging cutoff — prevents charging below approximately 32°F (0°C), protecting the cells.

Built-in self-heating — warms the cells before allowing solar charging.

Automatic recovery — resumes charging when the cells are warm enough, without someone visiting the cabin to reset it.

Solar-compatible heating — ideally uses incoming solar energy to warm the battery rather than continuously draining stored energy.

Cold-weather discharge protection — prevents excessive discharge at very low temperatures.

A regular LiFePO₄ battery with only a low-temperature cutoff can survive the winter, but it may not accept any solar charge until temperatures rise.

Batteries I'd consider

SOK SK12V100H 12V 100Ah LiFePO4 Battery Bluetooth & Built-in…

My first choice for a small cabin

12V · 100Ah · Charger-powered heating

Designed to heat its cells using incoming charger or solar power, avoiding unnecessary battery drain. Confirm the minimum solar input required to start heating.

$369.00

LiTime LiHeat® 12V 100Ah Group 24 Dual-Mode Self Heating Lit…

12V · 100Ah · Dual-mode heating

Automatic heating from an external charger, plus optional battery-powered preheating. LiTime documents charging operation in ambient temperatures down to -4°F (-20°C). 
First Dual Mode Self-Heating Technology
+1

$368.99

100Ah 12V LiFePO4 Deep Cycle Batteries

12V · 100Ah · Integrated heating

Established off-grid battery option, but its heater uses battery power (approximately 28W when active). That makes it less attractive for an unattended winter without sufficient solar production. 
The Battle Born Educational Series
+1

$999.00

The catch with leaving it unattended

Even a heated lithium battery can fail to maintain power through winter if the panels are snow-covered, daylight is insufficient, or the solar charge controller cannot restart after the battery disconnects.

For example, a 28W heater operating continuously would consume approximately 672Wh per day, before accounting for cabin loads. Some heated batteries also have minimum charging-current requirements; LiTime's 24V 230Ah model specifies 15A to activate heating. 
The Battle Born Educational Series
+1

For an unattended installation, I'd use an insulated battery enclosure, a solar controller with cold-weather and BMS recovery compatibility, appropriately sized panels, and remote monitoring. I would also verify the manufacturer's minimum storage temperature, not just its operating temperature.

Two questions would determine which battery I'd actually recommend for your cabin:

How cold does it get? Around 0°F (-18°C), -20°F (-29°C), or -40°F (-40°C)?

Does the cabin need electricity all winter, or do you only want the battery to remain charged and ready when you return?

That second distinction is especially important: the best battery for winter storage isn't necessarily the best one for continuously operating an off-grid solar system.
